sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The characteristics of this Source are based essentially on literature models. Constraints to the models are provided by GPS data for horizontal displacement and by coastal uplift and geodetic data for vertical displacement. Nevertheless, the uneven distribution of these data led to a number of solutions for the geometry of the rupture plane. In particular, the models that take into consideration the coastal uplift require non-uniform slip in order to fit the data.
Among all models available in the literature we adopt the one which agrees best with CMT solutions and general geologic and seismologic observations. The slip estimate we report is an average obtained assuming uniform slip on a fault having the same geometry of that reported by Meghraoui et al. (2004).
To estimate the slip rate of this Source we took the shortening rate calculated by Meghraoui and Doumaz (1996) in the El Asnam area and corrected that value for the geometry of the fault. We assumed that the Boumerdes and El Asnam faults have the same long-term behavior for they belong to the same regional geologic system though they exhibit opposite dip direction.
We adopted a strictly-periodic recurrence model and used the slip rates to yield a recurrence interval.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
All models for the Boumerdes earthquake require a south-dipping fault plane. Faults with this geometry were previously unknown in that region, as the active faults are all north-dipping thrusts. The 1980 El Asnam earthquake, the most destructive earthquake in Algeria, was also generated by a north-dipping thrust.
Deverchere et al. (2005) suggest that the Boumerdes earthquake is evidence of the ongoing underthrusting of the Neogene oceanic domain below the Algerian margin, which might represent an incipient stage of subduction.
1) If the south-dipping solution is reliable, the Boumerdes fault might be part of an offshore system capable of moderate-to-large earthquakes, which runs parallel to the already known Tell system. Apparently this earthquake revealed unsuspected features of the Algerian margin, with strong implication for the seismic hazard of the region. Is this another fault system to investigate more carefully? Are there other active fault segments west and east of this Source?
2) Most slip distribution models for the Boumerdes fault predict that much of the dislocation was released in two distinct patches. These models rely on a single data point showing no uplift in the middle of a rather regular pattern of coseismic uplift. Does this single observation justify the two-patch solution?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Bounif et al. (2004)
The coastal mainshock of the 21 May 2003 Boumerdes earthquake was followed by a large number of aftershocks, the largest reaching Mw 5.8 on 27 May 2003. The authors investigated the mainshock, the first major aftershocks and about 900 smaller events recorded by temporary seismic stations using a master-event approach and the double difference (DD) method, thus providing accurate aftershock locations. The mainshock hypocenter was relocated using three major aftershocks (5.0<Mw<5.8) chosen as master events. The new mainshock location shifted on the coastline (36.83N, 3.65E) at 8-10 km depth. Earthquakes extended to about 16 km depth and delineate a N 55Ã‚Â°-60Ã‚Â°E trending and 45Ã‚Â°-55Ã‚Â° SE-dipping fault. It is the only significant events of the Tell Atlas of Algeria that was investigated in detail. Mainshock and aftershock relocations, the thrust focal mechanism (Harvard CMT: N 57Ã‚Â°, 44Ã‚Â°SE dip, 71Ã‚Â° rake) and the seismic moment of 2.86*1019 Nm together indicate that the earthquake source was a 50-km-long rupture that may appear at the sea floor 6 to 12 km off the coast into the Mediterranea Sea.
Meghraoui et al. (2004)
In this work the active deformation related to 21 May 2003 earthquake (Mw 6.9, northern Algeria) was modeled along the 55 km coastline between Boumerdes and Dellys, where coastal uplift marked by a continuous white band is visible. Most of measured points were collected using tape and differential GPS on rocky headlands. Leveling lines running parallel and orthogonal to the coast also provide the amount of uplift in the epicentral area. The uplift distribution shows an average 0.55 m along the shoreline with a maximum 0.75 m east of Boumerdes and a minimum close to 0 near Cap Djinet. The dislocation model predicts slip on a N 54Ã‚Â°E trending reverse fault dipping 50Ã‚Â°SE, in agreement with the CMT solution and with coastal uplift. The faulting characteristics imply a fault geometry with possible sea floor ruptures between 5 and 10 km offshore.
Yelles et al. (2004)
In this work, GPS measurements of horizontal coseismic displacements are used to provide new constraints on the rupture geometry. Modeling the data with a uniform dislocation on a rectangular fault in an elastic half-space the authors find that the rupture occurred on a reverse fault dipping 42Ã‚Â°S, with its upper edge 6 km offshore and lower edge 4 km inland. The amplitude distribution of the coseismic displacements indicates that the rupture did not reach the surface, at least in its western part. Offshore faults like that responsible for the Boumerdes earthquake could account for part of the Africa-Eurasia relative plate motion in the western Mediterranean and represent a significant seismic threat for Algeria.
Deverchere et al. (2005)
The active seismogenic fault system in the area of the 2003 Mw 6.9 Boumerdes earthquake, Algeria was investigated through high-resolution swath bathymetry and a seismic survey. The results indicate that the two main slip patches of the 2003 Mw 6.9 Boumerdes earthquake are spatially correlated with two segmented cumulative scarps recognized on the slope and at the foot of the margin. The overall geometry indicates the predominance of back thrusts. The authors suggest that this implies underthrusting of the Neogene oceanic crust below the Algerian margin, which might represent an incipient stage of subduction.
